title: Saul’s story is one of the most sobering warnings in Scripture.
paragraphs: Saul’s story is one of the most sobering warnings in Scripture.

Not because he began wicked.
But because he began humble.

When Saul first appears in the biblical story, he doesn’t look like a man hungry for power. In fact, he looks like the opposite. When the time came for Israel to recognize him as king, Saul was hiding among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:22).
That image alone is powerful.
The man God had chosen to lead a nation was literally hiding.
And when the prophet Samuel confronted Saul later in his life, he reminded him of something important:
“Though you were little in your own eyes, were you not made the head of the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17).
Saul began small in his own eyes.
He began with the kind of humility that many people admire. The kind that seems safe. The kind that feels like it could protect a person from pride.
But Saul’s story reveals a deeper truth:
A humble beginning does not guarantee a humble heart forever.
Something inside Saul slowly changed.
At first, the kingdom was new. The calling was heavy. Saul depended on God’s direction through Samuel. But over time, Saul began to shift from dependence to insecurity.
And insecurity is often more dangerous than open pride.
Because pride announces itself.
Insecurity hides… until it feels threatened.
The moment that revealed Saul’s heart came after one of Israel’s victories. The women of Israel sang a song that echoed through the streets:

“Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his tens of thousands.”
— 1 Samuel 18:7
It sounded like celebration.
But to Saul, it sounded like comparison.
Scripture says Saul was very angry and that the saying displeased him (1 Samuel 18:8).
And then Saul said something revealing:
“What more can he have but the kingdom?”
In that moment, jealousy was born.
But the truth is, jealousy didn’t begin that day.
The song only exposed what was already growing in Saul’s heart.
Jealousy is rarely about the other person.
It is usually about fear, identity, and insecurity colliding inside a heart that no longer feels secure in God’s calling.

Saul was still king.
He still had the throne.
He still had authority.
Yet someone else’s praise felt like personal loss.
That is one of the most dangerous places a person can reach spiritually:
When someone else’s blessing feels like your defeat.
From that point forward, Saul’s life slowly turned into a chase. Not a chase for God. A chase for David.
The man who once hid among baggage began throwing spears.
The king who was chosen to lead began being consumed by comparison and suspicion.
And the tragedy is that David was never Saul’s enemy.

David honored Saul.
David served Saul.
David even refused multiple opportunities to harm Saul when Saul was vulnerable (1 Samuel 24, 26).
But jealousy distorts vision.
When insecurity takes root, even loyal people begin to look like threats.
Saul’s downfall reminds us of something deeply important:
Your greatest enemy is not always the person rising near you.
Sometimes the real battle is the part of your heart that struggles to trust God when someone else is blessed.
Comparison has destroyed countless callings.

Not because people lacked gifting.
Not because they lacked opportunity.
But because they could not handle someone else being celebrated.
Saul could handle being chosen.
But he could not handle being outshined.
And that is a test many people fail without realizing it.
Can you celebrate someone else's victory when it happens near you?
Can you honor another person's success without feeling smaller?
Can you trust that God’s calling on your life is still secure even when someone else’s influence grows?
Saul never won that battle.
And the saddest part of Saul’s story is not just that he lost a kingdom.
It’s that he lost peace long before he lost the throne.

Jealousy robbed him of rest.
Suspicion robbed him of trust.
Fear robbed him of joy.
The man who once led Israel became tormented by the very insecurities he refused to surrender to God.
And this is the warning Saul leaves behind for every generation:
If you don’t surrender your insecurities to God, they will eventually rule you.
You can be anointed and still become insecure.
You can be called and still become jealous.
You can start humble… and still fall if humility is replaced with comparison.
But Saul’s story is not only a warning.
It is also an invitation.
An invitation to build our identity in something deeper than applause.
Because when your identity is rooted in God’s approval, someone else’s success does not threaten you.
It inspires you.
It reminds you that God is still working.
The safest heart is not the heart that started humble.
It is the heart that stays surrendered.
And the most powerful test of humility is not how low you bow when no one notices you…
It’s how pure your heart stays when someone else is rising beside you.
So the real question Saul’s story leaves us with is this:
When God begins to bless someone near you…
Will your heart celebrate?
Or will it compete?

“A heart at peace gives life to the body,
but envy rots the bones.”
— Proverbs 14:30
Let Saul’s story be a warning we take seriously.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual battles are not fought on battlefields.
They are fought inside the human heart.
And the victory that matters most is the one that keeps jealousy from ever sitting on the throne.
